proof:
# A sharp incidence threshold for three positive-circuit triangle caps

Let P be a nondegenerate planar triangle, let y be in its interior, and let

    H_i={w:n_i.(w-y)>=0}, i=1,2,3,

be closed halfspaces. Suppose n_1,n_2,n_3 span R^2 and there are strictly positive numbers omega_i such that sum_i omega_i n_i=0. Write q_i=|P intersect H_i|/|P| for ordinary area fractions. Put

    c_0=2 sqrt(3)-3.

**Theorem.** If q_i<=c<c_0 for all i, each H_i contains exactly one vertex of P, these three vertices are distinct, and no other vertex lies on any cap boundary. The threshold is sharp: at c=c_0 there is a positive-circuit menu with all three fractions c_0 and a cap boundary through another triangle vertex.

The theorem is an ordinary geometric statement. It asserts neither mixed-integer compatibility nor genuine mixed criticality. In particular it cannot be used to infer that an arbitrary middle body is triangular.

## 1. Rotating a two-vertex cap to a vertex cut

Call a vertex strictly captured when n_i.(P_j-y)>0. Every through-y halfspace strictly captures at least one vertex: otherwise its nonzero affine functional would be nonpositive at all vertices and zero at their strictly positive barycentric combination y, forcing zero at every vertex. A cap of area less than one cannot strictly capture all three vertices.

Suppose one cap strictly captures two vertices P_1,P_2 and excludes P_0. Write the source's barycentric coordinates at P_1,P_2 as alpha,beta>0. Its boundary intersects the edges from P_0 at fractions u,v in (0,1), respectively. These satisfy

    alpha/u+beta/v=1,
    v=beta u/(u-alpha),
    alpha/(1-beta)<u<1.

The omitted corner has relative area uv. The captured fraction is therefore

    Q(u)=1-beta u^2/(u-alpha),
    Q''(u)=-2 beta alpha^2/(u-alpha)^3<0.               (1)

Keep the other two cap normals fixed. They are linearly independent: opposite normals would have cap fractions summing to one, and equal-direction normals could not participate in a rank-two positive circuit. The directions of the moving normal which form a positive circuit with them are exactly the interior of the cone generated by their negatives. This is an open angular interval of width less than pi. The cap directions in the displayed two-vertex incidence class also form an open angular interval of width less than pi; u parametrizes this interval continuously and strictly monotonically. Their intersection containing the present cap is an open interval in u.

By strict concavity in (1), choose one direction in u along which Q never increases until the endpoint of that interval: if Q'>=0 choose decreasing u, and otherwise choose increasing u. If Q'=0, either direction immediately strictly decreases Q. The interval endpoints are finite and the endpoint cap exists, because y is interior and alpha/(1-beta)>0.

The endpoint cannot be a positive-circuit boundary. At such a boundary, the moving normal is a negative multiple of one fixed normal, so the two limiting closed caps have areas summing to |P|. Both fractions would be at most c<1/2, a contradiction. Thus the endpoint is an incidence boundary: its line passes through one of P_1,P_2, while the other is strictly captured. The positive circuit is retained, and the moving cap's area has not increased.

Apply this operation successively to every cap which still strictly captures two vertices. At most three operations are needed, because previously modified caps are held fixed. If the original menu contained a two-strict-vertex cap, the final menu has at least one line through a triangle vertex. If instead the original failure was already a cap with one strictly captured vertex and another boundary vertex, retain that cap throughout.

At the end, every cap strictly captures exactly one vertex. Every triangle vertex must be strictly captured by some cap: if all three normal evaluations at a vertex were nonpositive, their strictly positive weighted sum zero would force all evaluations to be zero. Rank two would then force that vertex to equal y, which is impossible. Therefore the three strictly captured vertices are distinct.

We have proved the following reduction entirely by actual cap rotations:

> If the theorem's incidence conclusion fails for a menu with all q_i<=c<1/2, there is another positive-circuit menu through the same source, still with all fractions <=c, such that each cap strictly captures a different vertex and at least one cap line passes through another vertex.

No body deformation, affine lattice normalization, or minimizer-shape assertion enters this reduction.

## 2. Barycentric lower bounds for canonical vertex caps

Consider a cap strictly capturing vertex P_j and no other vertex strictly. Let alpha,beta be the source barycentric coordinates at the other two vertices. Its edge intercept fractions u,v belong to (0,1], and

    alpha/u+beta/v=1,
    q=uv.

The inequality uv=alpha v+beta u>=2 sqrt(alpha beta uv) gives

    q>=4 alpha beta.                                  (2)

There is a useful boundary refinement. If alpha>=1/2, write

    uv=beta u^2/(u-alpha).

For u<=1<=2alpha its derivative beta u(u-2alpha)/(u-alpha)^2 is nonpositive. Consequently

    q>=beta/(1-alpha).                                (3)

It follows that a distinct-vertex three-cap menu with all fractions <1/2 has all three source barycentric coordinates <1/2. Indeed, if one source coordinate alpha were >=1/2, the caps at the other two vertices would, by (3), have fractions at least beta/(1-alpha) and gamma/(1-alpha). Their sum is one, so one is at least 1/2.

## 3. Exact obstruction at a vertex cut

Use the reduced menu from Section 1, and label its boundary cap so that it strictly captures P_1 and its line passes through P_2. Let the source barycentric coordinates at P_1,P_2,P_3 be x,y,z. They are positive, sum to one, and by Section 2 are all less than 1/2.

The boundary cap has one edge intercept equal to one and the other equal to z/(x+z). Thus

    q_1=z/(x+z).

The other two caps satisfy (2), hence

    q_2>=4xz,   q_3>=4xy.                              (4)

Set t=z/x. Since q_1<=c<1/2,

    0<t<=r:=c/(1-c)<1,
    1/[2(1+t)]<x<1/2,
    y=1-(1+t)x.                                       (5)

If t<=1/2, the concave function 4xy=4x-4(1+t)x^2 has on the closed interval [1/(2(1+t)),1/2] minimum at an endpoint. Its endpoint values are 1/(1+t) and 1-t, both at least 1/2. This contradicts q_3<=c<1/2.

Thus t>1/2. The increasing function 4t x^2 and the concave function 4x-4(1+t)x^2 meet at

    x_* =1/(1+2t),
    J(t)=4t/(1+2t)^2.

This meeting point lies between the endpoints in (5). If x>=x_*, the first function is at least J(t). If x<=x_*, concavity bounds the second function below by the smaller of its values at 1/(2(1+t)) and x_*. The former is 1/(1+t)>=J(t), so again the maximum is at least J(t). Therefore (4) implies

    c>=max(q_2,q_3)>=J(t)>=J(r)
      =4c(1-c)/(1+c)^2,                               (6)

because J decreases for t>1/2. Dividing by c>0 and rearranging gives

    c^2+6c-3>=0,
    c>=2 sqrt(3)-3.

This contradicts c<c_0 and proves the theorem, including exclusion of positive-mass-free boundary vertex incidences.

## 4. Sharpness and the specific threshold 128/279

Let s=sqrt(3), and choose any triangle with barycentric coordinates lambda_1,lambda_2,lambda_3. Set the source coordinates to

    x=(s-1)/2,
    y=z=(3-s)/4.

Define affine through-source cap margins by

    f_1=(s/2) lambda_1-lambda_3,
    f_2=-x lambda_1+lambda_2-(1/s)lambda_3,
    f_3=-x lambda_1-(1/s)lambda_2+lambda_3.

All vanish at the chosen source, and

    (2/3) f_1+(1/s) f_2+f_3=0.

Their normals span the plane, so they form a positive circuit. The first cap captures P_1 and has P_2 on its boundary. Its fraction is z/(x+z)=c_0. The other two are the minimizing vertex caps with intercepts (2x,2z) and (2x,2y), respectively, so each fraction is 4xz=4xy=c_0. This proves sharpness.

Finally

    128/279 < 2 sqrt(3)-3,

because (128/279+3)^2=(965/279)^2<12, with exact numerator gap

    12*279^2-965^2=2867>0.

Thus the theorem applies directly to the ordinary three-cap fraction bound 128/279. It requires no additional joint cap-profile inequality.
